name: Piracetam
lead: Piracetam is the original racetam, a synthetic nootropic first made in the 1960s by Corneliu Giurgea at UCB in Belgium and the compound for which the word "nootropic" was coined.[1][2] People who take it do so mainly for focus, memory and mental sharpness, which feeds into how they look through the chain of better studying and work output, steadier routines and, in some stacks, recovery from head-related fatigue; it has no direct effect on skin, hair or bone structure.

It is a cyclic derivative of GABA, taken by mouth, and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys.[2][7] It is prescribed in the UK for cortical myoclonus and in many European and other countries for cognitive decline, vertigo and related complaints, while in the United States it is not FDA-approved and its inclusion in supplements is unlawful.[1][2]

Research includes clinical trials in dementia, mild cognitive impairment, stroke, aphasia, vertigo, dyslexia and concussion, plus reviews of nootropic use by healthy people and students.[3][4][6][7][8][14][15] Results vary by condition and by review, and trials in healthy people are limited.

chain: Used for focus, memory and mental energy
More consistent studying, training and routine
angle.text: Piracetam is used as a cognitive supplement, so its link to looks runs through routine: people stack it with training, study and sleep protocols hoping for more focus and mental stamina. It does not act on skin, hair or physique directly.

infobox: Rx in UK and Australia; not FDA-approved in US; OTC in some countries[1]

paras: Piracetam has no direct cosmetic use. Looksmaxxing-adjacent users take it as a general cognitive aid to support focus on studying, work and self-improvement routines, sometimes alongside choline sources or other racetams.[3][4]

In the UK it is approved for adults with cortical myoclonus, and in a number of European countries it is sold for age-related cognitive decline, vertigo and post-stroke problems.[1][7] Japan lists it as prescription-only, while the Czech Republic and Hungary sell it over the counter.[1]

Piracetam was synthesised in 1964 at the Belgian pharmaceutical company UCB by a group led by Corneliu Giurgea, a Romanian psychologist and chemist who was born in Bucharest in 1923, trained in Bucharest and St. Petersburg, did postdoctoral work at the University of Rochester and later taught at the Catholic University of Louvain while working as a scientific adviser at UCB.[1][18][2] Wikipedia notes reports of related work in the 1950s.[1]

Giurgea coined the word nootropic in 1972, and his published criteria describe a drug that improves learning and memory, helps memories withstand disruptions such as electroconvulsive shock or low oxygen, protects the brain against chemical or physical insults, strengthens cortical and subcortical control mechanisms, and has few side effects and very low toxicity without the sedating or stimulating effects of typical psychotropic drugs.[18] Piracetam was the compound that defined the category, and it became the founding member of the racetam family.[18][6]

Racetams share a 2-pyrrolidone core, and many have the 2-oxo-1-pyrrolidine acetamide structure of piracetam; they are cyclic relatives of GABA.[20] The nootropic members include piracetam, oxiracetam, aniracetam, pramiracetam, phenylpiracetam and others, while levetiracetam, brivaracetam and seletracetam are used as anticonvulsants.[20]

No single mechanism is universally accepted. Piracetam and aniracetam have been described as positive allosteric modulators of AMPA receptors, the anticonvulsant racetams bind the SV2A protein, and phenylpiracetam is described as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor.[20] In animal studies, piracetam's effects on cognition in aged rats were reported to increase when it was combined with choline, which is the origin of the common pairing with choline sources in user stacks.[20] Australia schedules all racetams as prescription-only (Schedule 4).[20]

Giurgea first used the word nootropic in 1972, combining the Greek words for mind and turning.[19] Wikipedia notes there is no globally accepted clinical definition and that most compounds sold as nootropics do not meet his original criteria.[19]

Regulators have repeatedly addressed the supplement market around these compounds. The FDA issued warning letters to supplement makers in 2010, the American Medical Association adopted a 2016 policy discouraging nootropic prescriptions for healthy people, and the FDA and FTC issued a joint warning in February 2019 about marketing scams involving nootropic supplements.[19] Studies reported piracetam in mislabelled supplements in 2020 and unapproved drugs in cognitive-enhancement supplements in 2021.[19][1] In the US, supplements may not contain drugs or make disease claims, and the FDA has stated that some racetam products are drugs rather than dietary supplements.[19]

Wikipedia's nootropic article summarises the literature on healthy people as follows: stimulants such as caffeine, low-dose amphetamine and methylphenidate show modest effects on some functions in meta-analyses, a 2015 review of modafinil reported improved executive function in small studies, and for racetams there is little evidence of cognitive enhancement in people without impairment, though serious adverse effects are few.[19] The 2022 review of smart drugs in healthy individuals and a 2021 systematic review of student cognitive-enhancer use take the same population as their subject.[3][4]

Wikipedia summarises piracetam's status by country: the FDA has not approved it and it may not lawfully be included in dietary supplements or compounded drugs in the US, even though it has been sold in the gray market for decades; it is prescription-only in the UK, where it is approved for adult cortical myoclonus, and in Australia (Schedule 4) and Japan; it is available without prescription in the Czech Republic, and in Hungary a 600 mg product (Memoril Mite) has been over the counter since 2020; and in Canada it has no drug identification number so cannot be sold, though personal importation is allowed.[1]
Brand names include Nootropil, Breinox, Dinagen, Lucetam, Nootropyl and Oikamid.[1]

Wikipedia reports that a 2001 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for dementia or cognitive problems, that a 2005 review described some benefit in older people with cognitive impairment, and that a 2008 UK Academy of Medical Sciences working group considered many dementia trials flawed; evidence for vascular dementia is described as insufficient.[1] The 2022 review of smart drugs in healthy individuals discusses piracetam-type compounds among nootropics whose effects in unimpaired people remain under study.[3]

Early controlled trials examined piracetam in chronic brain failure in older adults and in post-concussional syndrome, reporting outcomes in memory, symptom scores and daily function.[9][10] A 1986 report reviewed its effects in developmental dyslexia, and a 1991 randomized trial studied it in elderly motorists.[11][16]

A 12-month registered trial enrolled 676 people with mild cognitive impairment, and a 1998 trial of 571 people tested it for aphasia after middle cerebral artery stroke; the latter was terminated.[14][15] Reviews of vertigo treatment have assessed its effectiveness, and a trial compared it with dimenhydrinate in peripheral vertigo.[12][17] A 2012 Cochrane review examined its use for fetal distress in labour.[13]

Reviews of nootropics in healthy people describe popularity among students and workers and note that effects in non-impaired brains are still being assessed.[3][4] Wikipedia summarises Cochrane and other reviews, including a 2001 review that found insufficient evidence in dementia.[1]

Among the registered studies, a 12-month trial in mild cognitive impairment and a trial in post-stroke aphasia are the largest, and smaller registrations examine tardive dyskinesia, diabetic neuropathy, post-COVID symptoms and vertigo.[14][15][17] A 2020 JAMA Internal Medicine analysis by Cohen and colleagues found piracetam in products sold as cognitive-enhancement supplements.[1]

Reported effects include anxiety, insomnia, irritability, headache, agitation, tremor, drowsiness and weight gain.[1] Because it reduces platelet aggregation, it is contraindicated in cerebral haemorrhage, and dose reduction is advised in kidney impairment since elimination slows.[1][2] Acute toxicity in animals is very low.[1]

No single mechanism is established.[6] Proposed actions include weak positive modulation of AMPA receptors, effects on cholinergic and NMDA systems, calcium channel inhibition, improved membrane fluidity and better red blood cell deformability.[1][2][6][8]
Oral absorption is nearly complete, with peak plasma levels about an hour after a fasted dose and a plasma half-life near five hours; it is not significantly metabolised.[2]

Piracetam (2-oxo-1-pyrrolidine acetamide) is a white crystalline powder very soluble in water.[2] It was synthesised in 1964 at UCB, initially as an analogue explored for motion sickness, and marketed from 1971 as a cognitive enhancer.[1][2] It founded the racetam family, which includes aniracetam, oxiracetam and phenylpiracetam, and is structurally related to the antiepileptic levetiracetam.[6]

In the United States piracetam is sold through gray-market channels despite lacking FDA approval.[1] A 2020 study found racetam-type drugs in cognitive-enhancement supplements.[1] A systematic review of student use lists piracetam among drugs taken as study aids.[4]

lore.intro: Piracetam is discussed as the original nootropic and as a baseline for racetam stacks.[3]

claims.claim: Piracetam sharpens focus and memory in healthy people
claims.believers: Users and supplement marketers describe a boost to studying and mental clarity, often combined with choline sources.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews of nootropics in healthy individuals say effects in people without impairment are still being assessed, and the 2001 Cochrane review on dementia found insufficient evidence.[3][1]

claims.claim: Piracetam is a safe, low-toxicity compound
claims.believers: Proponents point to the low toxicity in Giurgea's original criteria.[18]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists anxiety, insomnia, irritability, headache and tremor as reported effects and notes it is contraindicated in cerebral haemorrhage because it reduces platelet aggregation.[1]

claims.claim: Piracetam works best stacked with choline
claims.believers: Users commonly pair racetams with a choline source and describe headaches without it.[3]
claims.experts: The pairing traces to rat studies in which piracetam's effects in aged animals increased with choline.[20]

claims.believers: Sellers market racetams as dietary supplements.[1]
claims.experts: The FDA says some racetam products are drugs, not supplements, and has issued warning letters.[19]

card.summary: The original racetam nootropic, taken for focus and memory to support study, work and training routines.
card.note: Not FDA-approved in the US; reduce intake with kidney impairment.

quick.overview:
Piracetam is the first of the racetams, developed at UCB in the 1960s. It is taken by mouth and prescribed in parts of Europe for cognitive decline, vertigo and myoclonus.

People in self-improvement communities take it for focus and memory, which supports their study, training and routine consistency rather than changing appearance directly.
quick.mechanism: Its mechanism is not settled. Proposed actions include mild AMPA receptor modulation, effects on acetylcholine and NMDA signalling, and improved blood cell flexibility and microcirculation.
quick.risks: Reported effects include anxiety, insomnia, irritability, headache and agitation. It lowers platelet aggregation, so it is contraindicated in brain haemorrhage, and kidney impairment slows clearance. It is prescription-only in the UK and not FDA-approved in the US.
